title: I rebuilt my portfolio into a studio. Here’s everything that broke.
excerpt: From one 766 KB HTML file to a Next.js site with its own admin, price estimates and a 3D gallery. The decisions, the bugs and what I learned.
coverAlt: The 3D gallery hall on my portfolio
blocks: For most of this year my portfolio was one file. A single index.html, 766 KB, holding eleven case studies, a journal and every animation. It looked finished. Under the surface it was fragile: changing one price or fixing one typo meant opening that file and hoping I didn't break something else.

In November I decided to turn it into something closer to a product: a site I could edit from an admin, that clients could get a price estimate from, and that still loaded fast on a slow phone in Abuja. This is the honest version of how that went.
Timeline of the portfolio from July to November 2026
Five months and nineteen commits, from one HTML file to launch day.
Why rebuild something that already worked

I'm starting a studio. A studio portfolio has a different job from a personal one. It has to answer the questions a founder asks before they message you: what would this cost, how long would it take, and how do you work?
My old site couldn't answer any of that without me editing code. So the goal wasn't a new look. I kept the design exactly as it was. The goal was everything behind it.
Diagram: one HTML file on the left, Next.js, Supabase, an admin and a studio funnel on the right
The design stayed the same. What changed is everything you don’t see.
The decisions, and why I made them
Next.js, so pages are built once and served instantly instead of being assembled on every visit.
Supabase on its free plan, for posts, case studies, prices, briefs and visit counts, with a small check-in so the free project never goes to sleep.
My own admin with email and password, because I design admin systems for clients and wanted to live inside one myself.
No heavy extras on the public pages. If something is big, like the 3D gallery, it only downloads when someone asks for it.

I didn't rewrite eleven case studies by hand. I wrote small scripts that read the old file and turned each section into a component, so the markup and the behaviour stayed identical. Migration scripts are boring, and boring is exactly what you want when you're moving something that already works.
Four problems: every page 404, the brief form crashing, a Git question loop, and a password that couldn’t be shown
Four things that broke on the way to launch.

Launch day went wrong straight away. Every page returned 404. The cause was one missing line telling Netlify how to run Next.js. I rolled back to the old site in a minute, added the line, and pushed again.

Then the first person to send a brief got “This page couldn’t load”. The live site didn't have the database keys yet, so it tried to save the brief to a file on a server that doesn't allow writing files. Now the keys are in place, and if saving ever fails the visitor gets a friendly message with my email and WhatsApp instead of a crash.

Some problems were just unfamiliar. Git on Windows kept asking “Should I try again? (y/n)” forever. I couldn't log in to my own admin because Supabase never shows passwords, by design. Each one felt like a wall for ten minutes and a lesson afterwards.
Most bugs weren't hard. They were invisible until the moment a real person used the thing.
The studio part: an estimate in two minutes

The new Services page lets someone pick what they need, how big it is and how their team works. A timeline and a price range update as they go, in naira or dollars. When they send the brief, it's saved in my admin, emailed to me and they can carry on the conversation on WhatsApp.
The Services page estimate changing as options are picked
Every choice updates the timeline and price range.
Story mode: six tries to get it right

I wanted visitors to feel my case studies, not just scroll past them. The first version was a scrolling story. Then a tap-through one. Then a cinematic one. Then a curved gallery room, inspired by an art site I loved. It still felt flat, so I built a full 3D hall you walk through in first person, one exhibit per case study, each with a short write-up and a Play story button.
Four versions of story mode side by side
From a flat gallery to a 3D hall. Every version taught me what the next one needed.
Walking through the 3D hall from one case study to the next
Walking the hall. It only downloads when someone switches Story mode on, and weak phones get a lighter version.
An admin I'd hand to a client

Everything is editable now: journal posts, case study text and covers, prices, homepage text and links. Briefs arrive with one-tap replies in Gmail or WhatsApp. There's a Visits page showing where people come from and which case studies they open, without cookies or storing anyone's IP address.
The case study editor in the admin
Editing a case study. Empty fields keep the designed text.
What I'd tell a founder (or a recruiter)
Four steps: ask, prototype, test on a phone, ship once
The loop I followed every day.
I ask before I assume. One question with three options saves a day of rework.
I prototype where nothing is at risk. Every Story mode version was tested on a private page before it touched the live site.
I test on a phone, on a normal network. If it's slow there, it isn't done.
I ship in one batch and check the live result myself. Hosting credits are real money, so I don't push every small change.
I'm a product designer learning to build what I design. This rebuild was the biggest step so far, and I documented every lesson in the code so I understand why each line is there.
Want something built like this, or want me on your team?

title: I kept forgetting to drink water in the heat, so I designed and built HeatBud
excerpt: With El Niño in the news and my days packed with work, I kept noticing the heat only after it had already got to me. So I made a small app to warn me first, and it’s live today.
coverAlt: Three HeatBud app screens on a warm orange background
blocks: For weeks, everyone around me was talking about El Niño.
Hotter months. Drier air. Afternoons that feel heavier than the number on the weather app.
And I was too busy to notice any of it.
My days are mostly back-to-back design work. I’d look up mid-afternoon with a dull headache, realise my bottle was still full, and only then notice how hot the room had become.
That’s when it clicked: I wasn’t short of weather information. I was short of a nudge at the right time.
Every weather app I opened gave me a number. 34°. 36°. Partly cloudy.
But a number doesn’t tell you what to do with it. Is it safe to go out at 1 PM? Should I move that errand to the evening? How much water do I actually need today?
A weather number is data. What people need in the heat is a decision.

And I’m one of the lucky ones who works indoors. Millions of Nigerians spend their whole day outside: riders, traders, builders, delivery staff, students walking to class. For them, heat isn’t an inconvenience. It decides how the day goes.
So I designed a buddy, not a dashboard
I gave myself a few rules before drawing a single screen:
Lead with how hot it feels, not the air temperature, because humidity changes everything.
Always say what to do next, in one plain sentence.
Make it feel like it was made here: Abuja on screen, Nigerian time, everyday English.
Keep it friendly. Heat is serious, but fear doesn’t make people open an app twice.
HeatBud home screen showing feels-like temperature over an illustrated Abuja scene
Home: how hot it feels, the risk level, and one sentence telling you what to do.

Open HeatBud and the first thing you see is the feels-like temperature over an illustrated Abuja scene, with a rating from Safe to Dangerous and a line like “OK with precautions until about 11 AM. Carry water, wear a hat, keep to shade.”
Underneath sits a heat dial, the best time to go out today, and a water bottle that fills up as you drink.
The water bottle took three tries
My first idea filled the whole Water page like a glass. It looked fun in a mockup. In use, it took over the screen and buried everything else.

So I moved water tracking onto Home as a real bottle with a side scale, the way you’d check one on your desk. The Water tab now holds the plan: a schedule across your day, with more water during the hottest hours, marked “do not skip.”
HeatBud heat dial and water bottle tracker
The bottle tells you how far behind you are and how much to drink now.
Your target comes from your weight, how active you are and the day’s forecast. Someone doing manual work outside gets a very different plan from someone at a desk.
The part I didn’t expect: safety
“Drink more water” sounds like harmless advice. It isn’t for everyone. People with heart, kidney or liver conditions, or on water pills, can be harmed by drinking too much.
So HeatBud asks. If a doctor has set a fluid limit, the app keeps your target inside it, and there’s a short guide to the warning signs of heat illness.
Designing for health means designing for the person the feature could hurt, not just the person it helps.
HeatBud is also my first serious build. I’m learning to code by making things I designed myself, and this one taught me fast.

Push notifications were the hardest part. On the web they need a server and the right permissions on every phone. Dragging my files onto Netlify kept breaking that, so I learned to deploy from the command line instead. I also added calendar alarms as a backup, so reminders still fire with the app closed and no server involved.
HeatBud settings with twelve buddy characters
Pick a buddy, set your routine, and add a doctor’s fluid limit if you have one.
And yes, there are twelve buddies. Sunny, Spike the cactus, Melon, Gecko and friends. Small things like that are why people come back.
HeatBud is live. It opens on any phone and installs to your home screen like an app. It has five tabs: Home, Forecast, Water, Alerts and Me.

It isn’t finished, and I don’t want it to be. Next I’m working on more reliable push alerts, more realistic landmark scenes, and, most of all, feedback from people who actually spend their day in the sun.
Try HeatBud on your phone and tell me what would make it more useful for you.
Want the full design story, with every screen and decision?
Stay cool out there. And drink some water. Your buddy says so.

title: AI can design a screen in ten seconds. That’s exactly why you still need a designer.
excerpt: Last month a founder showed me 40 screens he’d generated over a weekend. They looked great. None of them answered the one question his users were asking.
blocks: A founder sent me a Figma link on a Monday morning.
“I did the whole app over the weekend with AI. Can you just polish it?”
Forty screens. Clean spacing. Nice gradients. Honestly, it looked better than a lot of first drafts I’ve seen from people.
Then I asked him one question: “What should a new user do first?”
He scrolled for a while. He couldn’t point to it. Neither could the app.
Making screens is no longer the hard part
This is the shift nobody really talks about. AI didn’t make design easy. It made making things easy.

You can now produce a hundred good-looking screens before lunch. What you can’t produce that fast is the judgement behind them: which ten screens actually matter, what to cut, what your users don’t trust yet, and what will fall apart when a real person with a slow phone and a full inbox tries to use it.
When everyone can make something that looks finished, deciding what it should be becomes the real work.
More of my work has quietly moved from “design this for me” to “help me make sense of what I already have.” In practice that means:
Looking at what a team has generated and saying, kindly but clearly, what to keep and what to throw away.
Finding the one flow that decides whether people stay, and making that flow excellent before anything else.
Turning a pile of screens into a small system, so the product still feels like one product six months from now.
Bringing the context a prompt can’t: who your users are, what they’ve been burned by, and how they really pay, share and sign up.
That last one matters a lot here. Most AI tools learned design from products built for other markets. If your users are in Lagos, Nairobi or Johannesburg, the defaults are often quietly wrong.
I use it every day. It helps me explore faster, write rough copy, and test ideas I’d never have had time for.
But a tool that can make anything still needs someone to decide what’s worth making. That’s the job now.
If you’re sitting on a folder of AI screens and a quiet feeling that something isn’t right, that’s my favourite kind of conversation. Let’s talk.

title: Nobody told me the hardest part of designing a savings app would be fear
excerpt: I thought I was designing for people who wanted to save money. I was really designing for people who had already lost it.
coverAlt: Savings app screens on a blue background
blocks: Ten minutes into a research call, a woman stopped answering my questions and started telling me a story.
Years ago she’d joined a savings group with people she trusted. One day the person holding the money stopped picking up calls.
“So,” she said, “why would I trust an app?”
I didn’t have an answer. That was the moment the KOYNX project changed for me.
People had heard every promise already
Almost everyone we spoke to had a version of that story. A group that collapsed. An app that suddenly froze withdrawals. A friend who “would pay back next month.”
Big words like “secure” and “guaranteed” didn’t calm anyone down. They’d heard all of that before.
Trust isn’t something you say. It’s something people can check, again and again, without asking you.
So we stopped promising and started showing
Put the boring details right where people look: when the money unlocks, and what happens if you need it early.
Let group members see who has paid this round, so nobody has to chase anyone.
Show the name on the receiving account before the PIN, so there’s no doubt about where money is going.
None of these were exciting to design. All of them came straight from people’s fears.
Next time you start a fintech project, ask people about money they’ve lost, not just money they want to save.
Their answers will show you exactly which screens need to work hardest.

title: I built my first design system backwards. Here’s what I’d do instead.
excerpt: I started with buttons and cards. Three weeks later I had three versions of every button and a developer who had stopped asking me questions.
coverAlt: Dashboard screens built from a shared design system
blocks: Three products. One small team. One deadline that didn’t care about either.
I did what felt natural: I designed the components first. Buttons, cards, inputs. Beautiful ones.
Then the admin dashboard needed tighter tables. The mobile app needed bigger tap areas. Every “small exception” created a new version of something.
Within a few weeks the system wasn’t a system. It was a collection.
The fix was making decisions before shapes
I went back and started with tokens: the small, named decisions underneath everything. Which colour means “do this.” How much space sits between related things. How big a heading is.
Each product could then use those same decisions at its own size. Same language, different density.
If a developer has to ask which grey to use, the system has already let them down.
Naming things by how they look (“blue-500”) instead of what they do (“action-primary”). One brand change meant editing hundreds of layers.
Writing the documentation in a separate file nobody opened. Notes inside the components did more than any handbook.
If you’re starting a system this month, start smaller than feels right. Ten good decisions beat a hundred pretty components.

title: I’m a designer learning to code. Week one humbled me in a way I didn’t expect.
excerpt: I thought the hard part would be the syntax. It was realising how many of my designs were missing half their screens.
coverAlt: A web portal interface on screen
blocks: I’ve “started learning to code” more times than I’d like to admit.
A bit of C years ago. Some terminal commands. Tutorials I finished without really understanding.
This time I made one rule: only build things I designed myself. If I write a line of code, I should know exactly why it’s there.
The first thing code taught me had nothing to do with code
In Figma, a screen is a picture. In code, a screen is the result of some information: who the user is, what they’ve done, what’s still loading.

const screen = !user ? "loading" : user.posts.length ? "feed" : "empty";

// three screens. I had designed one.
That one line showed me two screens I had never drawn. The waiting one, and the empty one.
Learning to code didn’t make me less of a designer. It showed me which parts of my designs were just wishful thinking.
Design the loading, empty and error screens next to the main one, not later.
Name layers the way a developer would name things.
Put rough work on a live link early, even when it’s embarrassing.
If you’re a designer thinking about learning to code: start with something you already designed. It hits differently.

title: The hardest part of refreshing a school’s brand was deciding what not to change
excerpt: Everyone had an opinion. Alumni loved the old look, parents wanted clarity, students just wanted the portal to work.
blocks: When people hear “rebrand,” they picture a shiny new logo.
When I started working on a college’s brand, my first job was the opposite. I had to figure out what people would be upset to lose.
A school brand belongs to a lot of people
Former students remember the colours from their uniform. Parents remember the fees page. Current students mostly remember whether the portal let them log in.
A brand refresh that only pleases the marketing team won’t last a semester.
So I went looking for what was already working
I collected everything: signs, social posts, the website, printed forms, the student portal. The name and colours were genuinely recognised. That was worth protecting.
What felt tired was everything around them: too many fonts, random icons, and a homepage trying to say ten things at once.
Kept the colours, but gave them clear rules.
Went from four fonts to one family.
Gave announcements a proper home, so admission news stops taking over everything.
A good refresh makes people think “they got their act together,” not “who is this?”
My test was simple: can a former student recognise the college’s post in their feed before reading the name? If yes, we kept what mattered.

title: Five people broke my onboarding in one afternoon. Best afternoon of the project.
excerpt: I was proud of those eight setup questions. By question four, every single tester was tapping skip without reading.
blocks: For WeMove, a fitness app, I designed an onboarding I was genuinely proud of.
Eight thoughtful questions. Clean layout. Friendly copy.
Then I watched five real people use it.
By question four, everyone was tapping “Skip” without reading. One person said, “I just want to see a workout.”
Why I test with five people, not fifty
Five people won’t tell you everything. But they’ll show you the biggest problem almost immediately, and that’s what you need first.
Find five people who actually match your users, not your colleagues.
Give one simple task: “Set this up so it’s useful to you.”
Watch. Say nothing. The awkward silences are where the lessons are.
Fix the top three problems, then do it again.
Testing isn’t about proving your design works. It’s about finding out where it doesn’t, as early and cheaply as possible.
We cut onboarding down to three questions and moved the rest into the first week of using the app. The one question we kept up front was the one that mattered most: how active are you right now?

title: “I just need a logo.” Why I usually say no to that first.
excerpt: Most small businesses don’t lose customers because of their logo. They lose them because nothing they post looks like it comes from the same place.
blocks: Nearly every new brand enquiry I get starts the same way.
After years of freelance work, I now reply with a question: where will people actually see your business this month?
The answer is usually a WhatsApp status, a few Instagram posts, a flyer and maybe a shop sign.
The logo isn’t what makes those work
It helps. But what makes people remember you is seeing the same colours, the same tone and the same feel everywhere they meet you.
What I suggest starting with instead
One sentence that says what you do and who it’s for.
Two brand colours and one neutral. Used every single time.
One font for headings, one for everything else.
Three ready-to-use templates: a post, a status and a flyer.
Then the logo, designed to sit comfortably inside all of that.
Consistency beats cleverness. A simple mark used everywhere does more than a brilliant one used once.
If you’re a small business owner reading this, look at your last five posts side by side. Do they look like they came from the same business?

title: The day I realised my developer didn’t understand my Figma file
excerpt: “Is Card/Large the same as Tile/Primary?” It was. I just never told anyone, and the names didn’t either.
blocks: Halfway through a build, my developer sent me a message.
“Quick one. Is Card/Large the same as Tile/Primary?”
They were the same thing. I’d just named them on different days, in different moods.
That question cost us an afternoon. Multiply it across a project and you lose weeks.
Names are the cheapest documentation you’ll ever write
Name things by their job, not their look: “PaymentSummary,” not “BlueCard.”
Agree on one word with your developer and use it in both Figma and code.
Use variants for state and size: default, pressed, disabled; small, medium, large.
If a name needs explaining, it’s the wrong name.
A design system is a shared language. The names are its vocabulary.
After one afternoon of renaming, the questions almost stopped. Even better, my developer started suggesting names in the comments. That’s when you know you’re speaking the same language.

title: My app had five screens in Figma and twenty on a real phone
excerpt: The first time I shipped something myself, the internet in Abuja taught me more about design than any tutorial.
blocks: In Figma, my little web app had five screens. All of them looked perfect.
Then I opened it on my phone, on a normal Abuja network, and watched it struggle.
Half-loaded images. A blank white screen for four seconds. A button I tapped twice because nothing seemed to happen.
Offline: what still works, and how do you say so without scaring anyone?
Slow: a grey outline of the page feels faster than a spinning circle.
Half-loaded: the text arrived, but one image didn’t.
First visit vs. returning: the same screen with two very different jobs.
A design isn’t finished when it looks right. It’s finished when it still feels right on a bad connection.
Now I draw the empty, loading and error screens beside every main screen, before I call anything done.
That’s the real reason I want to become a design engineer. Not to replace developers, but to hand them designs that already know how they’ll be used.
